pos: n. pl. (plural of foot; rendering Hebrew regel, Greek pous)
etymology: Plural of foot, from the Saxon fot, an old irregular plural formed by vowel change rather than by adding -s. Hebrew regel is the foot and also, by extension, a journey or a time — three regalim a year Israel went up to the feast.
biblical_def: Feet in Scripture mark station, service, and submission, and the Bible's attention to them is remarkable for a book so little interested in physical description. To sit at a teacher's feet is to be a disciple, and Luke records it of a woman as a matter of course: Martha's sister Mary “sat at Jesus' feet, and heard his word” (Luke 10:39), the posture of a student, which our Lord defends as the good part. To wash feet is the lowest household service, reserved for the least slave, and it is the office the Lord of glory takes: he “poureth water into a bason, and began to wash the disciples' feet” (John 13:5). Feet also carry the gospel, and Isaiah's praise of them is one of Scripture's warmest sentences: “How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace” (Isaiah 52:7) — beautiful not in themselves but for what they bring, the dusty feet of a runner with news. Paul completes the picture by arming them: “your feet shod with the preparation of the gospel of peace” (Ephesians 6:15). The soldier's footing in the whole armour is the gospel, and a man who is unsure of it cannot stand.
webster_summary: The plural of foot. In Scripture the mark of discipleship (sitting at the feet), of lowest service (washing them), and of the messenger — beautiful are the feet of him that publisheth peace.
webster_full: FEET, n. plural of foot. [Sax. fot.] The parts of the body on which an animal stands or walks.
2. Steps or manner of walking; conduct; as, order my steps in thy word.
3. To sit at the feet of, to be a disciple or learner.
4. To wash the feet, an office of hospitality and of the lowest service, John 13.
5. In Scripture, of a messenger; as, how beautiful are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, Isa. 52.
corruption_summary: Service is now measured by visibility and scope, so the smallest tasks are delegated to whoever is least important. Christ took the basin himself, and told the twelve that they had a pattern rather than a spectacle.
corruption_paragraphs: The disciples had been disputing which of them should be greatest, and John 13 is the answer given without a lecture. The washing of feet was so degrading that Jewish servants were not required to perform it, and it was done at the door on arrival, not during supper — the timing itself shows the twelve had all walked past the basin. He rose from supper and did it. Then he said, if I then, your Lord and Master, have washed your feet, ye also ought to wash one another's feet.

The principle to recover cuts against a persistent instinct in ministry, where leadership is imagined as elevation and the work of a church is ranked by prominence. Isaiah 52:7 calls the feet of the messenger beautiful, and feet are the part that gets dirty; the beauty is borrowed entirely from the tidings. A congregation that honours the visible gifts and quietly despises the ones that involve basins has inverted the order its Lord established on the last night of his life.
roots_summary: Hebrew regel is foot, and by extension a journey or a festival pilgrimage. Greek pous is foot, giving podos in compounds, and nipto is the verb for washing a part of the body, used of the feet in John 13.
roots_lines: Hebrew regel (H7272) — foot; also a time or occasion, as in the three annual feasts.
Hebrew paam (H6471) — a step, a foot, a time; the tread of a foot and a repeated occasion.
Greek pous (G4228) — foot; used of sitting at the feet of a teacher and of washing feet.
Greek nipto (G3538) — to wash a part of the body; distinguished from louo, to bathe wholly.
Greek hupopodion (G5286) — a footstool; until I make thine enemies thy footstool, Psalm 110:1.
usage: Of the posture of a disciple: Mary, which also sat at Jesus' feet, and heard his word (Luke 10:39).
Of the lowest service taken by the Lord: began to wash the disciples' feet (John 13:5).
Of the messenger of the gospel: how beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings (Isaiah 52:7).

pos: n. pl. (plural of tooth; rendering Hebrew shen, Greek odous)
etymology: Plural of tooth, from the Saxon toth, formed like feet and geese by vowel change. Hebrew shen is a tooth and also an ivory or a sharp crag, and the law of retaliation — tooth for tooth — uses it as the measure of exact and limited justice.
biblical_def: Teeth in Scripture figure violence, extremity, and finally judgment. As weapons they belong to the wicked and to the beasts, and the Psalmist prays for God to disarm them: “thou hast smitten all mine enemies upon the cheek bone; thou hast broken the teeth of the ungodly” (Psalm 3:7) — breaking the teeth is not cruelty but the drawing of a predator's fangs. Job gives the language its most quoted phrase for narrow survival: “My bone cleaveth to my skin and to my flesh, and I am escaped with the skin of my teeth” (Job 19:20). Proverbs uses teeth for the small persistent irritation of an unreliable man: “As vinegar to the teeth, and as smoke to the eyes, so is the sluggard to them that send him” (Proverbs 10:26). Their gravest use is our Lord's. Six times in the Gospels he describes the place of judgment as one of “weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matthew 8:12), and gnashing in Scripture is the sound of rage rather than of remorse — Stephen's murderers gnashed on him with their teeth. Hell in Christ's own account is not repentance at last but hostility unended, which is why it is eternal.
webster_summary: Plural of tooth. Figures the weapons of the violent, the narrowest escape (the skin of my teeth), and above all the judgment our Lord names weeping and gnashing of teeth.
webster_full: TEETH, n. plural of tooth. [Sax. toth.] The bony processes in the jaws, used for biting and chewing.
2. The teeth of a saw, comb, or wheel; anything resembling a tooth in form or use.
3. To cast in one's teeth, to reproach or upbraid.
4. The law of retaliation; as, an eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth, Exod. 21.
5. In Scripture, of judgment; as, there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth, Matt. 8.
corruption_summary: Hell is widely reimagined as annihilation, or as remedial, or as a metaphor. Our Lord described it more often than anyone in Scripture, and his repeated image is weeping and gnashing of teeth — grief joined to unbroken rage.
corruption_paragraphs: Annihilationism, universalism, and the post-mortem second chance all soften the same texts, and all founder on the words of Christ. He is the one who speaks most about the place, and the phrase he repeats is not merely sorrowful but hostile: gnashing of teeth is what the enemies of Stephen did in Acts 7 while they stoned him, and what the wicked do against the righteous in Psalm 37. The lost in our Lord's descriptions are not penitents held back from a mercy they now desire; they are still gnashing.

That observation answers the most common objection to eternal punishment, which asks how a finite life can deserve an unending penalty. Matthew 8:12 suggests the sin does not stop. The principle to recover is that our Lord's own severity is the measure here, and no doctrine of hell is safe that is gentler than his words. The same mouth that said weeping and gnashing of teeth also said come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and the two are not in competition; the warning is the reason the invitation is urgent.
roots_summary: Hebrew shen is a tooth, an ivory, or a sharp crag, and appears in the law of exact retaliation. Greek odous is a tooth and brugmos is the gnashing or grinding of them, the noun our Lord uses of judgment.
roots_lines: Hebrew shen (H8127) — tooth, ivory, crag; the measure in tooth for tooth.
Hebrew charaq (H2786) — to gnash or grind the teeth; what the wicked do against the just.
Hebrew malteah (H4973) — the great teeth or jaw teeth; break out the great teeth of the young lions.
Greek odous (G3599) — a tooth; used in the retaliation formula and in the judgment phrase.
Greek brugmos (G1030) — a gnashing, a grinding; joined to weeping in our Lord's descriptions of hell.
usage: Of God disarming the violent: thou hast broken the teeth of the ungodly (Psalm 3:7).
Of the narrowest escape: I am escaped with the skin of my teeth (Job 19:20).
Of the place of judgment: there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth (Matthew 8:12).

My bone cleaveth to my skin and to my flesh, and I am escaped with the skin of my teeth. and

pos: n. pl. (drops shed in weeping; rendering Hebrew dimah, Greek dakruon)
etymology: From the Saxon tear, a tear. Hebrew dimah is a tear or tears collectively, from a root meaning to weep; the noun is regularly used with verbs of pouring, as though tears were a drink offering, which is close to the sense of Psalm 42, my tears have been my meat day and night.
biblical_def: Tears are treated in Scripture with a seriousness the modern world reserves for achievements. They are counted: “Thou tellest my wanderings: put thou my tears into thy bottle: are they not in thy book?” (Psalm 56:8) — the image is of a small flask kept by a mourner, and David asks God to be that keeper, so that no grief of his people goes unrecorded. They are sown: “They that sow in tears shall reap in joy” (Psalm 126:5), which makes weeping a kind of agriculture, an investment whose harvest is certain though delayed. They belong to faithful ministry, and Paul makes them part of his defence at Miletus: “by the space of three years I ceased not to warn every one night and day with tears” (Acts 20:31) — a pastor who never wept over his people had not warned them as Paul did. And they have an appointed end, which is one of the last promises in the Bible: “God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain” (Revelation 21:4). The tears are not denied, dismissed, or explained; they are wiped away, and by God's own hand.
webster_summary: Drops shed in weeping. Scripture has God collect them in a bottle, makes them seed for a certain harvest, marks faithful ministry by them, and promises that God himself will wipe them away.
webster_full: TEARS, n. plural of tear. [Sax. tear.] The limpid fluid secreted by the lachrymal gland and appearing in the eyes, especially in weeping.
2. Grief; sorrow; as, a house of tears.
3. Any transparent drop of fluid matter; as, tears of gum.
4. In Scripture, put thou my tears into thy bottle, Psa. 56; they that sow in tears shall reap in joy, Psa. 126.
5. Of their end; as, God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes, Rev. 21.
corruption_summary: Tears are managed as a symptom — a process to complete or a weakness to master. Scripture keeps them, counts them, and promises that they will be wiped away by the hand of God rather than merely stopping.
corruption_paragraphs: The therapeutic frame treats grief as a task with stages, and the stoic frame treats it as a lapse of composure; both leave the mourner alone with it. Psalm 56:8 offers something neither can: God as the keeper of the flask. The verse assumes tears are worth keeping, which is a claim about their meaning, not merely a comfort about their acceptability. And Psalm 126:5 refuses the notion that weeping is wasted time — it is sowing, and the harvest is promised, not hoped for.

The principle to recover is where Scripture puts the end of tears. Revelation 21:4 does not say the redeemed will get over their griefs or reinterpret them; it says God shall wipe them away, an act of personal tenderness, and then lists what will be abolished — death, sorrow, crying, pain. Until then Christians weep, and Acts 20:31 shows that faithful pastoral labour weeps too. A ministry with no tears in it has usually stopped warning anybody about anything.
roots_summary: Hebrew dimah is tears, from dama, to weep. Greek dakruon is a tear, and exaleipho is the strong verb in Revelation 21:4 — to wipe out, to obliterate, the same word used of blotting out sins.
roots_lines: Hebrew dimah (H1832) — tears; what David asks God to gather into his bottle.
Hebrew bakah (H1058) — to weep aloud; the verb behind the noun.
Hebrew nod (H4997) — a skin bottle, a flask; the vessel of Psalm 56:8.
Greek dakruon (G1144) — a tear; used of the tears God shall wipe away.
Greek exaleipho (G1813) — to wipe out, to blot out; used both of tears and of the handwriting against us.
usage: Of God keeping account of grief: put thou my tears into thy bottle (Psalm 56:8).
Of weeping as sowing: they that sow in tears shall reap in joy (Psalm 126:5).
Of their promised end: God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes (Revelation 21:4).

pos: n. (the breast; the place of intimacy and safekeeping; rendering Hebrew cheq, Greek kolpos)
etymology: From the Saxon bosm. Hebrew cheq is the fold of the garment at the breast, where a shepherd carried a lamb and a man carried what was precious — so the word means the place of nearest keeping before it means a part of the body.
biblical_def: Bosom denotes the place of closest intimacy and safest keeping, and Scripture puts three of its greatest statements there. Of the Trinity: “No man hath seen God at any time; the only begotten Son, which is in the bosom of the Father, he hath declared him” (John 1:18) — the eternal nearness of the Son to the Father is the reason he can make the Father known, and revelation therefore rests on relation. Of God's care for the weakest of his flock: “He shall feed his flock like a shepherd: he shall gather the lambs with his arm, and carry them in his bosom” (Isaiah 40:11), where the strong arm that gathers and the bosom that carries belong to the same God who in the preceding verses measures the waters in the hollow of his hand. Of the state of the righteous dead before the resurrection: the beggar “died, and was carried by the angels into Abraham's bosom” (Luke 16:22), a phrase for blessed rest in the company of the father of the faithful. Proverbs uses the word for the folly of harboured sin: “Can a man take fire in his bosom, and his clothes not be burned?” (Proverbs 6:27) — what is carried closest will do the most damage.
webster_summary: The fold at the breast — the place of intimacy and safekeeping. The Son is in the bosom of the Father; the Shepherd carries lambs in his; and Lazarus was carried into Abraham's.
webster_full: BOSOM, n. s as z. [Sax. bosm.] The breast of a human being, and the parts adjacent.
2. The folds or covering of clothes about the breast; a place of safekeeping.
3. Embrace; inclosure; compass; as, in the bosom of the church.
4. Intimacy; nearest affection; as, a bosom friend.
5. In Scripture, the only begotten Son, which is in the bosom of the Father, John 1; carried into Abraham's bosom, Luke 16.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The word has faded from ordinary speech, and with it the picture of a shepherd carrying a lamb inside the fold of his robe.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The loss is imaginative. A modern reader hears bosom as archaic or awkward, and Isaiah 40:11 flattens into a general reassurance. The picture is specific: a shepherd's outer garment was gathered by a belt so that the fold across the chest formed a pouch, and a newborn or injured lamb travelled there, against the man's ribs, unable to walk and not required to. Isaiah places this immediately after the verses on God's incomparable greatness, and the juxtaposition is the point.

The principle to recover is what John 1:18 grounds. The Son who declares the Father is the Son who has eternally been in his bosom, so Christian revelation is not information relayed by a messenger but disclosure by one who has always been at the Father's side. That is why he can say he that hath seen me hath seen the Father. And Proverbs 6:27 supplies the sober counterweight, that the bosom is also where a man hides what will ruin him: sin cherished close is not contained by being hidden, and the clothes burn.
roots_summary: Hebrew cheq is the bosom or the fold of a garment, the place of carrying; chob is likewise the breast. Greek kolpos is the bosom, the fold of a robe, and by extension a bay or gulf.
roots_lines: Hebrew cheq (H2436) — bosom, the fold of the garment; where a shepherd carried a lamb.
Hebrew chob (H2243) — the bosom; used in Job of what is hidden in the breast.
Greek kolpos (G2859) — bosom, lap, the fold of a garment; also a bay of the sea.
Greek monogenes (G3439) — only begotten; the Son who is in the bosom of the Father.
Greek exegeomai (G1834) — to lead out, to declare fully; he hath declared him, John 1:18.
usage: Of the Son's eternal nearness as the ground of revelation: which is in the bosom of the Father (John 1:18).
Of the Shepherd's care for the weakest: he shall gather the lambs with his arm, and carry them in his bosom (Isaiah 40:11).
Of the blessed dead: was carried by the angels into Abraham's bosom (Luke 16:22).

pos: n. (the state of being unclothed; exposure, shame; rendering Hebrew erwah, Greek gumnotes)
etymology: From naked, Saxon nacod, with the abstract ending -ness. Hebrew erwah means nakedness and, by a settled idiom, sexual dishonour — to uncover the nakedness of is the law's phrase for illicit union, so the word carries moral weight in the Hebrew itself.
biblical_def: Nakedness in Scripture is a state before God before it is a state before men. In Eden it was innocent and unremarked; after the fall the first consequence recorded is that the man and his wife knew they were naked, and God clothed them with skins, which required a death. From that point nakedness signifies exposure and shame, and covering it is an act of mercy. The law makes uncovering nakedness the standing phrase for sexual sin, and Genesis records the sin of Ham in exactly this register: he “saw the nakedness of his father, and told his two brethren without” (Genesis 9:22) — the offence being not only the seeing but the publishing, while Shem and Japheth walked backward to cover it. Paul lists nakedness among the afflictions that cannot separate the believer from Christ: “shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword?” (Romans 8:35). And the risen Christ diagnoses a wealthy church as naked without knowing it, counselling Laodicea to buy of him “white raiment, that thou mayest be clothed, and that the shame of thy nakedness do not appear” (Revelation 3:18). The remedy throughout Scripture is the same: a covering God provides.
webster_summary: The state of being unclothed — and in Scripture, exposure and shame before God. The remedy is always a covering God provides, from the coats of skins in Eden to the white raiment offered to Laodicea.
webster_full: NAKEDNESS, n. [from naked; Sax. nacod.] Want of covering or clothing; nudity; bareness.
2. Want of means of defense; as, the nakedness of the land, Gen. 42.
3. Plainness; openness; want of disguise.
4. In the law, a term for sexual dishonor; as, none shall approach to uncover their nakedness, Lev. 18.
5. In Scripture, the shame of thy nakedness, Rev. 3; God made coats of skins, and clothed them, Gen. 3.
corruption_summary: Shame at nakedness is treated as a repressive inheritance to be unlearned. Scripture treats the sense of exposure as a true signal of a real condition, and answers it with a covering God himself supplies.
corruption_paragraphs: The programme of unlearning bodily shame assumes that the sense of exposure is a cultural imposition, and that the cure is to feel it less. Genesis says otherwise. Adam and Eve were naked and not ashamed before they sinned, so shame is not native to the body; it entered with guilt, and it is therefore a truthful signal rather than a neurosis. Silencing the signal does not restore Eden. God's response was neither to shame them further nor to tell them the feeling was irrational: he made coats of skins and clothed them, and something died to do it.

The principle to recover runs from that first covering to Revelation 3:18. Laodicea was rich and increased with goods and did not know she was naked, which is the more dangerous condition — exposure without the sense of it. Christ's counsel is to buy white raiment of him, and the whole doctrine of imputed righteousness stands behind the figure: the covering is not manufactured by the naked party. Genesis 9:22 adds the duty of charity in the meantime, since Shem and Japheth were blessed for covering what Ham published.
roots_summary: Hebrew erwah is nakedness and sexual dishonour, and arom is naked. Greek gumnotes is nakedness, from gumnos, naked, the root of gymnasium, where the Greeks exercised unclothed.

Hebrew arom (H6174) — naked; they were both naked, the man and his wife, and were not ashamed.
Hebrew kasah (H3680) — to cover, to conceal; blessed is he whose sin is covered, Psalm 32:1.
Greek gumnos (G1131) — naked, bare; the root of gymnasium.
Greek gumnotes (G1132) — nakedness; listed among the afflictions of Romans 8:35.

Of affliction that cannot separate from Christ: famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword (Romans 8:35).

pos: n. pl. (paces; the course of a life; rendering Hebrew ashur and mitsad, Greek ichnos)
etymology: From the Saxon staepe, a pace. Hebrew ashur is a step or going, from a root meaning to go straight on; mitsad is a stride. Greek ichnos is a footprint — the mark left behind rather than the movement itself — which is the word Peter uses of following Christ.
biblical_def: Steps in Scripture stand for the actual course of a life, as distinct from its intentions, and the Bible's teaching here is one of its clearest statements of providence in ordinary things. Proverbs sets human planning and divine direction side by side without embarrassment: “A man's heart deviseth his way: but the LORD directeth his steps” (Proverbs 16:9). The man really devises; the LORD really directs; and the verse does not resolve the two into either fatalism or autonomy. The Psalter adds that this direction is a delight rather than a constraint: “The steps of a good man are ordered by the LORD: and he delighteth in his way” (Psalm 37:23), where the next verse promises that though he fall, he shall not be utterly cast down. Job appeals to the same accounting when his integrity is questioned: “Doth not he see my ways, and count all my steps?” (Job 31:4). And Peter gives the word its Christological turn, using the image of footprints in which to place one's own feet: Christ suffered for us, “leaving us an example, that ye should follow his steps” (1 Peter 2:21) — and the context is unjust suffering patiently borne, which is the specific path he means.
webster_summary: Paces — the actual course of a life. Scripture holds together a man devising his way and the LORD directing his steps, and calls believers to follow in the footprints of Christ.
webster_full: STEPS, n. plural of step. [Sax. staepe.] Paces; movements of the foot in walking.
2. Progression; course of life or conduct; as, to order one's steps aright.
3. Footprints; traces; as, to follow in another's steps.
4. Stairs; the rounds of a ladder; as, the steps of the throne.
5. In Scripture, the steps of a good man are ordered by the Lord, Psa. 37; that ye should follow his steps, 1 Pet. 2.
corruption_summary: Guidance is sought as a secret plan to be discovered before acting, or else denied altogether in favour of pure autonomy. Proverbs 16:9 grants real deliberation to the man and real direction to the LORD, in the same sentence.
corruption_paragraphs: Two errors bracket this doctrine. The paralysing one treats God's will as a hidden itinerary that must be located before any move is made, so that ordinary decisions become an anxious search for signs; a man in that condition cannot buy a house without a portent. The autonomous error simply plans and asks God to bless the result. Proverbs 16:9 will not license either. The heart devises — that is genuine, and Scripture everywhere expects believers to think, count the cost, and take counsel — and the LORD directs the steps, which is also genuine and is not diminished by the devising.

The principle to recover is that providence works through deliberation rather than around it, and that Psalm 37:23 adds the tone: the ordering of steps is the act of a God who delights in the man's way. That transforms the question a believer asks. Instead of hunting for a hidden plan, he walks in the revealed will of God with the mind God gave him, and trusts the direction of the steps to the One who counts them. Peter then names the one path Scripture explicitly calls us to tread — the steps of Christ, in patient suffering for well doing.
roots_summary: Hebrew ashur is a step or going, from a root meaning to go straight; mitsad is a stride, the word in Psalm 37:23. Greek ichnos is a footprint, and peripateo, to walk about, is the New Testament's standard figure for conduct.
roots_lines: Hebrew ashur (H838) — a step, a going; hold up my goings in thy paths, Psalm 17:5.
Hebrew mitsad (H4703) — a stride, a step; the word in the steps of a good man are ordered.
Hebrew tsaad (H6806) — a pace, a step; thou hast enlarged my steps under me.
Greek ichnos (G2487) — a footprint, a track; that ye should follow his steps, 1 Peter 2:21.
Greek peripateo (G4043) — to walk about, to conduct oneself; walk in newness of life, Romans 6:4.
usage: Of deliberation and providence together: a man's heart deviseth his way: but the LORD directeth his steps (Proverbs 16:9).
Of God's delight in the ordering: the steps of a good man are ordered by the LORD (Psalm 37:23).
Of following Christ in unjust suffering: leaving us an example, that ye should follow his steps (1 Peter 2:21).

Psalm 37:23
The steps of a good man are ordered by the LORD: and he delighteth in his way.

1 Peter 2:21
For even hereunto were ye called: because Christ also suffered for us, leaving us an example, that ye should follow his steps:

etymology: From like, Saxon lic, with the ending -ness. Hebrew demuth is from damah, to resemble, and is paired in Genesis 1:26 with tselem, image; the two words together resist the notion that man merely approximates God, and equally the notion that he duplicates him.
biblical_def: Likeness is resemblance, and Scripture uses it at three decisive points. At creation it defines what man is: “And God said, Let us make man in our image, after our likeness” (Genesis 1:26) — the plural us being one of the Old Testament's intimations of the Trinity, and the image being the ground of human dignity, of the prohibition of murder, and of the command not to curse men. At the incarnation the word guards a distinction of enormous consequence. God sent his own Son “in the likeness of sinful flesh, and for sin, condemned sin in the flesh” (Romans 8:3) — likeness of sinful flesh, not sinful flesh; real humanity, and no sin in it. Paul is equally careful in Philippians, where Christ “took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men” (Philippians 2:7) — the emptying is not the laying aside of deity but the taking on of servanthood. And at the last the word describes the believer's destiny: “I shall be satisfied, when I awake, with thy likeness” (Psalm 17:15). Man was made in God's likeness, defaced it in Adam, and shall be restored to it in Christ, of whom he is predestinated to be conformed to the image.
webster_summary: Resemblance. Man is made in God's likeness; the Son came in the likeness of sinful flesh — real humanity without sin; and the believer's end is to awake satisfied with God's likeness.
webster_full: LIKENESS, n. [from like.] Resemblance in form; similitude.
2. Resemblance in qualities or character; as, likeness of disposition.
3. A picture; an image; an effigy; as, to take a likeness.
4. One having a resemblance; a counterpart.
5. In Scripture, let us make man in our image, after our likeness, Gen. 1; in the likeness of sinful flesh, Rom. 8.
corruption_summary: The image of God is often reduced to a capacity — reason, or relationship, or dominion — and then quietly graded, so that some bearers count for more. Scripture grounds the dignity of every human being in the likeness itself.
corruption_paragraphs: Reducing the image to a function has consequences that arrive quickly. If the image is rationality, then the unborn, the senile, and the severely disabled hold it in lesser degree, and the argument for their protection weakens exactly where it is most needed. Genesis 9:6 grounds the prohibition of murder in the image without qualification — in the image of God made he man — and James forbids cursing men on the same ground, saying they are made after the similitude of God. The image is not a score.

The second and greater care is Christological. Romans 8:3 says likeness of sinful flesh, and the precision is deliberate: Christ took real human nature, subject to hunger, weariness, and death, but no sin, and the two clauses must both stand. Deny the likeness and you have docetism; deny the qualification and you have a Saviour who needed saving. The principle to recover is that this careful language is the hinge of the atonement: he had to be truly one of us to represent us, and truly sinless to be accepted for us.
roots_summary: Hebrew demuth is likeness, from damah, to resemble, and is paired with tselem, image. Greek homoioma is a likeness or resemblance, and eikon is the image, the word used of Christ as the image of the invisible God.
roots_lines: Hebrew demuth (H1823) — likeness, similitude; paired with image in Genesis 1:26.
Hebrew tselem (H6754) — image; in the image of God made he man, Genesis 9:6.
Greek homoioma (G3667) — a likeness, a resemblance; in the likeness of sinful flesh, Romans 8:3.
Greek eikon (G1504) — image; Christ is the image of the invisible God, Colossians 1:15.
Greek morphe (G3444) — form, essential nature; the form of God and the form of a servant, Philippians 2.
usage: Of the creation of man: let us make man in our image, after our likeness (Genesis 1:26).
Of the incarnation carefully stated: in the likeness of sinful flesh, and for sin, condemned sin in the flesh (Romans 8:3).
Of the believer's hope: I shall be satisfied, when I awake, with thy likeness (Psalm 17:15).
scriptures: Genesis 1:26

And God said, Let us make man in our image, after our likeness: and let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the fowl of the air, and over the cattle, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creepeth upon the earth.
Romans 8:3
For what the law could not do, in that it was weak through the flesh, God sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and for sin, condemned sin in the flesh:
Philippians 2:7
But made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men:
Psalm 17:15
As for me, I will behold thy face in righteousness: I shall be satisfied, when I awake, with thy likeness.

pos: n. (outward show; the act of becoming visible; rendering Hebrew mareh, Greek opsis and eidos)
etymology: From the Latin appareo, to come into view, through the French apparence. Hebrew mareh is what is seen, from raah, to see; the Hebrew has no separate word for mere appearance, so the contrast Scripture draws is always between what is seen and what God sees.
biblical_def: Appearance is what shows on the outside, and Scripture treats it as real but never as decisive. The classic text is spoken over Jesse's eldest son: “Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature, because I have refused him: for the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart” (1 Samuel 16:7). The rebuke is aimed at Samuel, a prophet, which shows how natural the mistake is even to godly men. Our Lord makes the same point a rule of judgment: “Judge not according to the appearance, but judge righteous judgment” (John 7:24) — a verse that both forbids superficial verdicts and plainly commands judgment of another kind, against the popular misuse of judge not. Paul adds a duty that runs the other way and is often set against these texts: “Abstain from all appearance of evil” (1 Thessalonians 5:22). Because appearances are not decisive for God, a believer is not to be governed by them; but because they matter to men, he is not to be careless with them either. The two sit together: do not judge by appearance, and do not create a damaging one.
webster_summary: Outward show. God looks on the heart and not on the outward appearance, and Christ forbids judging by it — yet Paul still commands abstaining from all appearance of evil.
webster_full: APPEARANCE, n. [L. appareo, to come in sight.] The act of coming into sight; the act of becoming visible.
2. The thing seen; a phenomenon; as, an appearance in the sky.
3. Semblance; apparent likeness; external show, as distinguished from reality.
4. Personal presence; exhibition of the person; as, a public appearance.
5. In Scripture, man looketh on the outward appearance, but the Lord looketh on the heart, 1 Sam. 16.
corruption_summary: An image-driven age makes appearance nearly everything, while a lazy reading of judge not makes discernment nearly impossible. Scripture denies that appearance is decisive and still commands care about it.
corruption_paragraphs: The first pressure is obvious: presentation has become a discipline, and churches are not exempt when they select leaders by platform presence rather than by the qualifications of 1 Timothy 3 and Titus 1, which are almost entirely matters of character and household. 1 Samuel 16:7 was spoken to correct precisely this instinct in a prophet who had just been impressed by a tall man. God's reason is not that appearance is unreal but that he sees something better — the heart — and chooses accordingly.

The second pressure is the misuse of judge not as a prohibition of all moral assessment. John 7:24 settles it in one sentence, since our Lord forbids one kind of judgment and commands another in the same breath: judge righteous judgment. Christians are to assess doctrine, conduct, and fitness for office, and to do so by the word rather than by the surface. The principle to recover is that 1 Thessalonians 5:22 completes rather than contradicts this. A man free from the tyranny of appearances is precisely the man who can afford to be careful about them for his neighbour's sake.
roots_summary: Hebrew mareh is the thing seen or the look of a thing, from raah, to see; ayin, the eye, supplies the idiom in the eyes of. Greek opsis is the visible aspect and eidos the outward form or fashion.
roots_lines: Hebrew mareh (H4758) — sight, appearance, visible form; what a thing looks like.
Hebrew raah (H7200) — to see, to perceive; the LORD seeth not as man seeth.
Hebrew lebab (H3824) — the heart; what God looks upon instead of the outward appearance.
Greek opsis (G3799) — the visible aspect, the face; judge not according to the appearance.
Greek eidos (G1491) — form, outward fashion, kind; the word in all appearance of evil.
usage: Of God's different sight: man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart (1 Samuel 16:7).
Of judgment forbidden and commanded in one breath: judge not according to the appearance, but judge righteous judgment (John 7:24).
Of care for how a thing looks to others: abstain from all appearance of evil (1 Thessalonians 5:22).
scriptures: 1 Samuel 16:7

But the LORD said unto Samuel, Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature; because I have refused him: for the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart.
John 7:24
Judge not according to the appearance, but judge righteous judgment.
1 Thessalonians 5:22
Abstain from all appearance of evil.
Psalm 17:15
As for me, I will behold thy face in righteousness: I shall be satisfied, when I awake, with thy likeness.

pos: a. and v. (tired, exhausted; to tire; rendering Hebrew yaeph, Greek kopiao and ekkakeo)
etymology: From the Saxon werig, tired. Hebrew yaeph is to be faint or exhausted, especially from travel or thirst; the same root gives the noun for the exhausted man in the desert whom Isaiah 32 promises shade as of a great rock in a weary land.
biblical_def: Weary describes exhaustion of body or spirit, and Scripture's treatment of it is notable for two things: it never rebukes the condition, and it always locates the remedy outside the weary man. Isaiah's argument runs by contrast. First the negative: “the everlasting God, the LORD, the Creator of the ends of the earth, fainteth not, neither is weary” (Isaiah 40:28) — God's inexhaustibility is stated as a doctrine of who he is. Then the promise built upon it: “they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint” (Isaiah 40:31). The order of the images descends from soaring to running to walking, which is the honest order of the Christian life, and walking without fainting is the hardest of the three. Jeremiah records God's own act toward the exhausted: “I have satiated the weary soul, and I have replenished every sorrowful soul” (Jeremiah 31:25). Paul then applies the word to the specific weariness of long obedience without visible result: “let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not” (Galatians 6:9). The promise is a harvest and the condition is not fainting.
webster_summary: Tired, exhausted. God fainteth not, neither is weary; those who wait on him renew their strength; and believers are charged not to grow weary in well doing, for the harvest is certain.
webster_full: WEARY, a. [Sax. werig.] Having the strength much exhausted by toil or violent exertion; tired; fatigued.
2. Having the patience exhausted; as, weary of waiting.
3. Causing weariness; tiresome; as, a weary way.
4. As a verb, to tire; to exhaust the strength or patience of; as, will ye weary my God also? Isa. 7.
5. In Scripture, they shall run, and not be weary, Isa. 40; let us not be weary in well doing, Gal. 6.
corruption_summary: Exhaustion is treated as a management problem to be optimised away, or as a failure of dedication. Scripture treats weariness as the ordinary condition of creatures and directs it to the God who does not grow weary.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The distortion is practical. On one side, a productivity culture treats tiredness as a defect to be engineered out, and the Christian version of this makes rest faintly suspect and drives faithful people until they break. On the other, weariness is offered as a reason to abandon a duty. Isaiah 40 answers both by putting the emphasis where neither does: on the character of God. The Creator of the ends of the earth fainteth not, and that is why waiting on him renews strength; the strength is transferred, not summoned.

The principle to recover is the realism of the sequence in Isaiah 40:31 and the patience of Galatians 6:9. Mounting up with eagles' wings comes first and is the rarest experience; running follows; and walking without fainting is last and longest, which is where most of the Christian life is actually lived. Paul's due season is God's season and not ours, so the weariness in view is precisely the weariness of not yet seeing the harvest. God does not tell such a man to try harder; Jeremiah 31:25 says he satiates the weary soul himself.
roots_summary: Hebrew yaeph is to be faint or exhausted, and yaga is to labour to weariness. Greek kopiao is to toil to the point of exhaustion, and ekkakeo is to lose heart or grow weary, the verb in Galatians 6:9.
roots_lines: Hebrew yaeph (H3287) — faint, weary, exhausted; used of a traveller and of a thirsty land.
Hebrew yaga (H3021) — to toil, to grow weary with labour; also of wearying God with words.
Hebrew qavah (H6960) — to wait, to look for with expectation; they that wait upon the LORD.
Greek kopiao (G2872) — to labour to exhaustion; come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden.
Greek ekkakeo (G1573) — to lose heart, to grow weary; let us not be weary in well doing.
usage: Of God's inexhaustibility: the Creator of the ends of the earth, fainteth not, neither is weary (Isaiah 40:28).
Of strength renewed by waiting: they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint (Isaiah 40:31).
Of long obedience without visible result: let us not be weary in well doing (Galatians 6:9).
scriptures: Isaiah 40:28
Hast thou not known? hast thou not heard, that the everlasting God, the LORD, the Creator of the ends of the earth, fainteth not, neither is weary? there is no searching of his understanding.
Isaiah 40:31
But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint.
Jeremiah 31:25
For I have satiated the weary soul, and I have replenished every sorrowful soul.
Galatians 6:9
And let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not.

pos: a. (afflicted with disease; ill; rendering Hebrew chalah, Greek astheneo)
etymology: From the Saxon seoc, ill. Hebrew chalah means to be weak or worn, and is used of bodily sickness and of a heart made faint; Greek astheneo is literally to be without strength, from a- and sthenos, and covers illness, weakness, and infirmity together.
biblical_def: Sick covers bodily illness and, by a natural extension, the sickness of a wearied heart. Scripture is direct about the church's duty toward the sick and equally direct that healing is not at the church's disposal. James gives the order of ministry: “Is any sick among you? let him call for the elders of the church; and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord” (James 5:14). The initiative lies with the sick man, the office with the elders, and the outcome with the Lord. Our Lord makes visiting the sick a mark of those he acknowledges at the judgment, and says it as though it were done to himself: “I was sick, and ye visited me” (Matthew 25:36). The message sent from Bethany is a model of how believers may speak to Christ about illness without dictating to him: “Lord, behold, he whom thou lovest is sick” (John 11:3) — a statement of fact and of relation, with no request appended; and he stayed two days where he was, and then raised the man. Proverbs applies the word to the inner life with exactness: “Hope deferred maketh the heart sick: but when the desire cometh, it is a tree of life” (Proverbs 13:12).
webster_summary: Afflicted with disease. Scripture makes visiting the sick a mark of Christ's own, gives the sick man the initiative to call the elders, and applies the word also to a heart made sick by hope deferred.
webster_full: SICK, a. [Sax. seoc.] Affected with nausea; inclined to vomit; also, in general, ill; indisposed; not in health.
2. Disgusted; having a strong dislike to; as, sick of flattery.
3. Corrupted; as, a sick state or constitution.
4. Languishing; longing; as, sick of love, Song 2.
5. In Scripture, is any sick among you? let him call for the elders of the church, James 5; I was sick, and ye visited me, Matt. 25.
corruption_summary: Sickness is claimed by prosperity teaching as always contrary to God's will and curable by faith, and treated by a secular frame as bare biology. Scripture puts it under providence and appoints prayer, elders, and visitation.
corruption_paragraphs: The teaching that healing is guaranteed to sufficient faith adds cruelty to affliction, since it makes every unhealed believer a failure. The New Testament will not carry it. Paul left Trophimus at Miletum sick, told Timothy to take a little wine for his stomach's sake and his often infirmities, and had his own thorn refused three times. Epaphroditus was sick nigh unto death, and Paul attributes his recovery to God's mercy rather than to anyone's technique. James 5:14 prescribes prayer and anointing by the elders, and the prayer of faith is offered in submission to God's will, not as a lever upon it.

The principle to recover is that Scripture assigns the church a duty rather than a power. Matthew 25:36 puts visiting the sick among the works our Lord names at the judgment, and he identifies himself with the sick person so completely that the visit is made to him. That is a far more demanding standard than a healing ministry, because it cannot be delegated to the gifted and it never becomes unnecessary. And John 11:3 teaches how to pray in the meantime: state the case, name the love, and leave the timing with him — even when he waits two days.
roots_summary: Hebrew chalah is to be weak, worn, or sick, used of the body and of the heart. Greek astheneo is to be without strength, and arrhostos is feeble or infirm; iaomai and therapeuo are the verbs of healing.
roots_lines: Hebrew chalah (H2470) — to be weak, sick, diseased; also of a heart made faint.
Hebrew machaleh (H4245) — sickness, disease; the affliction itself.
Greek astheneo (G770) — to be without strength, to be sick or weak; the word in James 5:14.
Greek arrhostos (G732) — feeble, infirm; used of those on whom Christ laid his hands.
Greek iaomai (G2390) — to heal, to cure; with his stripes we are healed, 1 Peter 2:24.
usage: Of the church's appointed ministry: is any sick among you? let him call for the elders of the church (James 5:14).
Of visitation as a mark of Christ's own: I was sick, and ye visited me (Matthew 25:36).
Of the heart under deferred hope: hope deferred maketh the heart sick (Proverbs 13:12).
scriptures: James 5:14
Is any sick among you? let him call for the elders of the church; and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord:
Matthew 25:36
Naked, and ye clothed me: I was sick, and ye visited me: I was in prison, and ye came unto me.
John 11:3
Therefore his sisters sent unto him, saying, Lord, behold, he whom thou lovest is sick.
Proverbs 13:12
Hope deferred maketh the heart sick: but when the desire cometh, it is a tree of life.
